title: Models, messages & prompts
summary: The base of every LLM application: **chat models**, **messages**, **multimodal input**, **prompt templates**, **structured output**, the ways to **invoke** a model, what to do when calls **fail**, **model profiles and reasoning models**, and **local models**. The production path builds **Nimbus support triage**: a customer message in, a validated routing decision out, scored on 20 labelled tickets.
learn: **Chat models**: `init_chat_model`, the AIMessage, tokens, and what temperature does
**Messages**: roles, why models are stateless, shorthand formats, saving and resuming a conversation
**Multimodal input**: images, several images, and PDF pages, as standard or provider-native blocks
**Prompt templates**: variables, history placeholders, partials, and few-shot examples, measured
**Structured output**: output parsers vs `with_structured_output`, Pydantic vs TypedDict, measured
**Invocation**: invoke, batch, stream and async, timed
**Errors**: timeouts, retries, and retry-later vs fix-the-request
**Model profiles and reasoning models**, and **local models** with Ollama
flow:
TICKET  →  prompt template (v2: rules + examples)  →  messages (+ photo if the model can see)
        →  chat model (configured client, rate limit, timeout, retries)
        →  structured output (TicketTriage, validated)  →  route  →  stream a reply draft
        →  evaluate: 20 labelled tickets → accuracy per field, tokens, cost

labs.explain:
Everything in LangChain starts with a **chat model**: `init_chat_model(name, model_provider=...)` gives one object with the same methods for every provider. Calling `invoke()` returns an **AIMessage**, not a string: `.text` is the answer, `.content` can be a string *or a list of blocks* (images, reasoning), `.usage_metadata` is the token count you are billed for, and `.response_metadata` says which model answered and why it stopped.

**Temperature** controls randomness. The lab asks the same question several times at 0 and at 1 and counts how many different answers come back.

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

code.why: Nimbus creates every model here: the provider and model are configuration.

notes.text: Temperature 0 by default: Nimbus classifies and extracts, so it wants the most repeatable answers.
A missing key fails at start-up with a clear message, not as a 401 on a customer's request.

code.why: One cached client per configuration.

notes.text: init_chat_model: one function for every provider; the provider package handles the HTTP API.

code.why: The lab: invoke at two temperatures.

notes.text: invoke() returns an AIMessage: .text, .usage_metadata and .response_metadata.
collect_runs records every model call with its start and end time: that's where the latency column comes from.

labs.explain:
A conversation is a **list of messages**: `SystemMessage` (instructions), `HumanMessage` (the user), `AIMessage` (the model). Models are **stateless**: they remember nothing between calls, so "memory" means your app stores the list and sends it again with every request, which costs more input tokens every turn.

LangChain also accepts **shorthand** (`("human", "hi")` tuples, `{"role": ..., "content": ...}` dicts, plain strings) and converts it. To resume a chat later, save the messages as JSON and load them back.

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

code.why: How Nimbus saves and resumes conversations.

notes.text: JSON back into SystemMessage / HumanMessage / AIMessage objects, metadata included.
The id becomes a file name: never let a request climb out of the folder.
Write to a temporary file, then rename: a crash never leaves half a conversation.

code.why: The lab: with and without the history.

notes.text: "Memory" is resending the list: the model itself keeps nothing.

labs.explain:
A message's content can be a **list of blocks**: text plus one or more images in the same message. Images go as **base64** data or as a **URL** the provider downloads. LangChain's **standard blocks** (`{"type": "image", "base64": ..., "mime_type": ...}`) work with every provider package; **provider-native** blocks (Mistral's `image_url`) are passed through as they are.

**PDFs:** render each page to an image and send it. That works with every vision model; native PDF input exists only on some providers. Every case in this lab is checked against the real file (the receipt total is ₹787.50; Q3 was the best quarter at 62 crore).

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

code.why: How a ticket's photo becomes a content block.

notes.text: A standard block: the same dict works with Mistral, OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini...

code.why: A ticket with an attachment becomes text + image in one message.

notes.text: Send the image only if the model's profile says it can read images.

code.why: A PDF page, rendered to an image.

notes.text: Render at 1.5× so small print stays readable; the image costs input tokens, so don't go higher than needed.

labs.explain:
A **ChatPromptTemplate** turns variables into messages: `template.invoke({...})` returns a **PromptValue** you can pass to any model, or turn into messages or a string. **MessagesPlaceholder** inserts a whole list (the chat history). **partial()** fixes some variables up front (the category list never changes per request). **Few-shot** examples are pairs of human and AI messages that show the model exactly what you want.

The lab compares Nimbus's prompt **v1 (zero-shot)** with **v2 (rules + 3 examples)** on six hard tickets, then shows what the examples cost in tokens.

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

code.why: The production prompts, versioned.

notes.text: Each example becomes a human message and an AI message: the model sees worked answers, not just rules.
v2 = the v1 instructions + routing rules + the examples. A new version, never an edit in place.
partial(): the category list is filled in once, so callers only pass the ticket.
The conversation so far is inserted here, as many messages as there are.

labs.explain:
Code needs **data**, not prose. Two ways to get it:

- **Output parsers** put format instructions into the prompt and parse the text that comes back: `StrOutputParser` (just the text), `JsonOutputParser` (a dict), `PydanticOutputParser` (a validated object, or an exception if the text doesn't fit).
- **`with_structured_output(schema)`** asks the provider for structured output, through **tool calling** or **JSON-schema mode**. A **Pydantic** schema returns a validated object, including **nested** lists; a **TypedDict** returns a plain dict nothing validates; `include_raw=True` hands you the raw AIMessage and any parsing error instead of raising.

The lab runs five methods on the same tickets with the same instructions, and compares accuracy, failures and tokens.

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

code.why: The schema: field types, allowed values and descriptions are all sent to the model.

notes.text: Descriptions are instructions: the urgency rules live in the schema itself.
A pattern the parsed value must match: an invented 'order 4410' fails validation.
Nested: a list of objects extracted from free text.

code.why: with_structured_output, as the lab runs it.

notes.text: include_raw=True: a dict of raw, parsed and parsing_error, instead of an exception.

code.why: An output parser, as the lab runs it.

notes.text: The parser reads the reply's text; nothing forced the model to follow the format.

labs.explain:
Every model (and every LangChain runnable) has the same methods:

- **invoke**: one input, one output.
- **batch**: many inputs, run concurrently (`max_concurrency` caps how many at once).
- **stream**: the output arrives in chunks as it's generated; chunks add up (`+`) to the full message.
- **ainvoke / abatch / astream**: the async versions, for async web servers.

The lab times a loop of `invoke()` against `batch()` and `abatch()`, and measures time to first chunk when streaming.

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

code.why: Nimbus triages a backlog concurrently.

notes.text: Concurrent calls, results in input order. batch() does the same, but only reports one total time.

code.why: The async version, for the web service.

notes.text: A semaphore bounds the calls in flight, like max_concurrency.

code.why: Reply drafts stream to the support agent.

notes.text: Each chunk is an AIMessageChunk; show its text as it arrives.

code.why: The lab: the same tickets, three ways.

notes.text: batch(): the calls overlap instead of waiting in line.

notes.match: full = chunk if full is None else full + chunk
notes.text: Chunks add up to one message: the same text invoke() would return.

labs.explain:
Model calls fail, and they fail in two very different ways:

- **Temporary** (timeouts, network errors, 429 rate limits, 5xx): retrying can work. The client retries them for you (`max_retries`, with backoff); `timeout` stops waiting after N seconds.
- **Permanent** (bad API key, unknown model, input too long): they fail at once, and retrying can never fix them.

Your code needs one decision per failure: **try again later**, or **fix the request**. The lab triggers each failure for real and classifies it.

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

code.why: Every model error, sorted by what to do about it.

notes.text: 429 and 5xx: temporary. Queue the work and try again later.
401, 400, 404: permanent. Retrying wastes time and money; alert someone.

code.why: One bad ticket must not stop the queue.

notes.match: one bad ticket must not stop the queue
notes.text: The failure becomes a result with an action, instead of an exception that kills the batch.

labs.explain:
**model.profile** is a dictionary of what a model can do: context size, image input, reasoning output, tool calling, structured output. When the provider package has no profile for a model (Ministral here), supply one yourself. Then check it in code: only send an image to a model that can read images.

**Reasoning models** think before answering and return the thinking as **reasoning** content blocks. `reasoning_effort` asks for more or less thinking: more thinking means more output tokens (billed) and more time. When streaming, the reasoning arrives first, then the answer. This lab uses `openai/gpt-oss-20b` on Groq's free plan (Mistral's reasoning model is rate-limited on its free plan: see the errors lab).

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

code.why: Profiles Nimbus fills in for models the package doesn't know.

notes.match: if chat.profile is None and model in KNOWN_PROFILES:
notes.text: The installed package has no profile for this model: use the one Nimbus keeps, from the provider's model card.

code.why: Check before sending.

notes.text: Unknown counts as no: never send an image on a guess.

code.why: The lab: three effort levels, then a stream.

notes.text: reasoning_effort is passed straight to the provider; supported values depend on the model.

labs.explain:
**Ollama** runs open models on your own computer as a small server, and LangChain talks to it like any provider: `invoke`, `stream`, tools and structured output, with only the model name changed. No API key, no rate limit, works offline, and your data never leaves the machine.

Small reasoning models (qwen3:1.7b) can switch **thinking off**, which makes them much faster. The lab compares cloud and local, tries tool calling, and swaps the production triager onto the local model unchanged.

Needs `ollama serve` running and `ollama pull qwen3:1.7b` (about 1.4 GB); the lab tells you if either is missing.

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

code.why: The local role: the same function, a different provider.

notes.text: Ollama, at the configured URL; no API key and no rate limiter needed.

code.why: The lab: cloud vs local, thinking on and off.

notes.text: reasoning=False turns off qwen3's thinking: far fewer tokens, much faster.

path.title: Production path: Nimbus support triage v1
path.summary: The support desk gets hundreds of messages a day in English, Hindi and Tamil. Triage reads each one and returns a validated decision (category, urgency, order id, language, whether a human must step in), then drafts a reply. Every choice below (prompt version, structured output method) was made with the scorecard in the last step.

steps.title: Model
steps.explain:
Every model call in Nimbus goes through `get_chat_model()`. The provider and model of each role (default, reasoning, local) are **configuration**, so switching provider is an environment variable, not a code change. Timeouts, retries and the client-side **rate limiter** are set once, and a missing API key fails at start-up.

The rate limiter is shared **per provider**: a provider counts every request from your key, whichever model it names, so two models with separate limiters would together exceed the limit.

code.why: The one entry point for every model call.

notes.text: Defaults first, then per-call overrides (a lab's temperature=1 gets its own cached client).
Fail fast and clearly when a key is missing.

code.why: Clients are cached: one per configuration.

notes.text: A new client per request would open new HTTP connections every time.
Every client of a provider shares that provider's limiter.

code.why: A token bucket per provider.

notes.text: 0.4 requests/s with bursts of 5: under Mistral's free-plan 30 requests/min.

production: With several server processes, an in-memory limiter only sees its own process: share one limit through Redis, or route calls through an LLM gateway.
Keep keys in a secret manager in production; `.env` is for local development, and it's git-ignored.
Log the model name and version with every call (`response_metadata`), so a quality change can be traced to a model change.

steps.title: Conversations
steps.explain: A support conversation spans many requests, and the model remembers none of them. Nimbus stores each conversation as JSON (LangChain's `messages_to_dict` format) and loads it back to continue. The reply prompt has a `MessagesPlaceholder` where the history goes.

code.why: Save, load and append.

notes.text: Validate the id before using it as a file name.
Atomic write: readers never see a half-written file.

production: Use a database table (one row per message, indexed by conversation id) once you have more than one server; the JSON format stays the same.
History grows with every turn, and so does the cost of every call: trim or summarise long conversations (LangChain Module 4: managing context).
Conversations contain personal data: set a retention period and delete on request.

steps.title: Prompts
steps.tagline: Versioned templates, chosen by the scorecard
steps.explain: Prompts are code: each change gets a **new version**, and the scorecard decides which one ships (`NIMBUS_TRIAGE_PROMPT_VERSION`). v1 is zero-shot; v2 adds routing rules and three worked examples. On the 20 labelled tickets v2 got **all fields right on 0.80** of them against **0.55–0.60** for v1 (two runs), for 448 more input tokens per ticket (measured with tool calling; see Evaluate).

code.why: Every prompt Nimbus sends.

notes.text: The edge cases v1 got wrong, written down as rules.
Three worked examples: a damaged order, Hinglish, an allergy emergency.
A new version next to the old one: both can be scored and compared.
The reply prompt takes the conversation so far.

production: Store the prompt version with every result, so a complaint can be traced to the exact prompt that produced it.
Never edit a shipped version in place: add v3, score it, then switch the setting.
LangSmith's Prompt Hub can hold versions outside the code (Shipping to production, Module 4).

steps.title: Triage
steps.tagline: A message in, a validated object out
steps.explain:
`Triager.triage()` builds the messages (with the ticket's photo when the model can read images), asks for a **TicketTriage** with `with_structured_output(..., include_raw=True)`, and returns a result that always has the raw reply, the latency, and either the parsed object or the reason it failed. Then `stream_reply()` drafts an answer token by token for the support agent.

**Run it** on any labelled ticket (the fields are checked against the label) or type your own.

code.why: The routing decision, as a schema.

notes.text: The urgency definition the model must follow.
The field the support desk routes on: wrong here means a customer waits.

code.why: Configured once, used for every ticket.

notes.text: JSON-schema mode by default: chosen by the scorecard (see Evaluate).

code.why: Text, plus the photo when the model can see.

notes.text: Checked against the model's profile, not assumed.

code.why: The reply draft, streamed.

notes.text: Skip empty chunks (the first chunk often carries only metadata).

production: Route on the validated fields only; keep `summary` for humans.
Record the raw reply and token usage of every triage for audits and cost tracking.

Customer text is untrusted input: it can contain instructions aimed at the model (prompt injection). Never let triage output trigger refunds or other actions without a check (LangChain Module 5: guardrails).

steps.title: Reliability
steps.explain: A backlog of tickets must survive a timeout, a rate limit or one malformed reply. `triage()` catches every failure and turns it into a result with an **action**: `retry` (temporary: put it back on the queue) or `fix` (the request or configuration is wrong: alert someone). A reply that doesn't match the schema is a `fix` result with the validation message, and the raw reply is kept for debugging.

code.why: Retry later, or fix the request.

notes.text: Temporary: 429 and 5xx.

code.why: Every outcome becomes a TriageResult.

notes.match: if out["parsing_error"] is not None or out["parsed"] is None:
notes.text: The model answered, but not in the schema: keep the raw reply, mark it 'fix'.
An exception: classify it into retry or fix.

code.why: A batch where one failure doesn't stop the rest.

notes.text: Each ticket succeeds or fails on its own.

production: Send `retry` results to a queue with exponential backoff and a maximum number of attempts; send `fix` results to an alert.
Set the timeout from measured p95 latency plus margin, not a guess: too short wastes the tokens already generated.
Add a fallback model for when the main provider is down (LangChain Module 2: fallbacks), and a circuit breaker (Shipping to production, Module 1).

steps.title: Evaluate
steps.tagline: Score every field routing depends on
steps.explain:
20 labelled tickets (Hinglish, Hindi, Tamil, legal threats, a chargeback, contamination, a missing order number) and a scorecard: **valid** (replies that matched the schema), **accuracy per field** (category, urgency, order id, language, needs_human), **all fields right** (what an agent never has to fix), **latency** p50/p95 (including time queued behind the rate limit), **tokens** and **cost per 1,000 tickets** at a reference paid price. Every run is added to the history.

Measured so far (Mistral ministral-14b):

| prompt · method | valid | all fields right | input tokens | $ / 1k tickets |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| v1 · tool calling | 0.95 | 0.55–0.60 | 583 | $2.02 |
| v2 · tool calling | 1.00 | 0.80 | 1,031 | $2.92 |
| **v2 · JSON schema** | **1.00** | **0.85** | **534** | **$1.87** |

So production uses **v2 with JSON-schema mode**: the rules and examples fixed urgency and needs_human, and JSON-schema mode kept that accuracy while sending the schema outside the prompt (36% cheaper than tool calling). Run it yourself: 20 model calls, about a minute under the free-plan rate limit.

code.why: Run the labelled tickets and score them.

notes.text: The production triager, exactly as it runs for real tickets.
The number that matters most: tickets an agent would never have to fix.

code.why: Exact match per field.

notes.text: A failed triage counts as wrong on every field.

production: Grow the labelled set from real tickets that agents corrected: they are exactly the cases the model gets wrong.
Run the scorecard in CI for every prompt, model or schema change, and block a release that lowers 'all fields right'.
Watch the same metrics on live traffic: the share of triages agents change is your real accuracy (Shipping to production, Module 4).
